description: Stella Nova is a solo project exploring space medicine and software development. I’m designing a health monitoring dashboard to track astronaut vitals and manage medical triage during long-term space missions. Competing individually allows me to independently push my limits in coding, data analysis, and healthcare research.
summary:
A heart-rate monitor can give you the wrong number without giving you a reason to doubt it. During exercise, wrist movement can interfere with pulse measurements, creating a serious challenge for astronauts who may need to monitor their health far from immediate medical support.

I developed Pulsar, an astronaut health-monitoring research demonstrator that combines wrist pulse signals with movement data to improve pulse estimation and assess measurement reliability. Rather than treating every reading as trustworthy, Pulsar investigates when uncertain measurements should be withheld for review.

Using real exercise recordings from eight participants, the research evaluated 332 measurement windows. Pulsar selected 125 readings for display, achieving an average error of 3.62 beats per minute among those displayed. An interactive application communicates these findings through recorded-data exploration and illustrative crew health check-ins.

Informed by NASA Human Research Program resources, Pulsar explores a vital principle for future space missions: health monitoring should help astronauts understand when to trust a measurement, not simply provide another number.
details:
Pulsar — Motion-Aware Astronaut Health Intelligence

Project: Pulsar | Team name: Stella Nova | NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026

Project overview

During an astronaut’s exercise session, repetitive wrist motion can alter the optical waveform used by a wearable heart-rate monitor. The displayed value may look plausible even when the sensor is tracking movement-related interference rather than a cardiac rhythm.

Photoplethysmography (PPG) estimates pulse rate from optical changes associated with blood volume. During physical activity, periodic arm movement can introduce components within the same frequency range as the heartbeat. The resulting ambiguity is difficult to resolve from a dominant spectral peak alone.

The question is relevant to human spaceflight: astronauts exercise regularly to help maintain physical conditioning, and future missions may have greater communication delays. Pulsar investigates how accelerometer-informed processing changes pulse-frequency estimation and how a separate error-risk rule can determine which candidate readings to display. Reporting accuracy and the availability of readings are assessed together.

Across 329 candidate-eligible terrestrial windows, motion-aware separation reduced mean absolute error from 36.35 to 21.69 beats per minute (bpm). The participant-held-out reliability policy displayed 125 of 332 windows (37.7% coverage), achieving 3.62 bpm mean absolute error among displayed readings while still accepting eight serious errors. These outcomes motivate careful accounting of both estimation error and withheld measurements.

Keywords: photoplethysmography; motion artifacts; accelerometry; selective prediction; abstention; astronaut health; measurement reliability.

1. Scientific problem and project objective

The study examines two connected questions: how motion-aware processing affects optical pulse-frequency estimates, and how a separate reliability assessment identifies readings that should be withheld. Its deliberate focus is measurement integrity, one component of an astronaut health-monitoring system rather than an attempt to provide comprehensive medical monitoring.

Synchronized wrist sensing, nonlinear motion modelling and frequency analysis generate the candidates. A separate error-risk policy determines research display status, which the crew check-in demonstrator makes understandable. The study evaluates how this decision changes both accuracy and coverage.

2. Technical methodology and architecture

2.1 Synchronized sensor analysis

The research pipeline examines simultaneous wrist PPG and three-axis accelerometer measurements in 20-second windows sampled at 256 Hz, yielding 5,120 samples per window. Optical variation associated with blood-volume changes is analyzed alongside movement on three spatial axes, enabling interference linked to wrist motion to be investigated.

2.2 Motion-aware separation

Nonlinear predictors are constructed from the accelerometer axes, their squared values, pairwise products, vector magnitude, and temporally shifted features. A blocked, out-of-fold ridge-regression procedure estimates the motion-associated component of the optical signal. The predicted component is subtracted to form a residual for candidate extraction.

The nonlinear motion basis accommodates cross-axis and time-delayed relationships. Because cardiac and motion frequencies can overlap, however, regression may suppress physiological information as well as interference.

2.3 Spectral candidates

Frequency-domain analysis identifies prominent peaks in the original optical signal and the motion-separated residual, producing alternative pulse-frequency candidates in bpm. Temporal consistency and motion-related signal properties provide additional diagnostic information. A stable peak can also originate from repetitive movement. Its suitability for reporting is assessed in the next stage.

2.4 Reliability model and selective reporting

The offline Python study uses an ExtraTrees classifier to estimate the risk that a candidate differs substantially from a reference electrocardiogram (ECG). An absolute difference of at least 15 bpm defines a serious error for this experiment; it is not a clinical alert threshold. Participant-held-out evaluation and training-derived acceptance cutoffs are used to examine whether candidates should be cautiously displayed or withheld for review.

Scores are uncalibrated and cannot be interpreted as probabilities of physiological correctness. The evaluation consequently reports error among accepted candidates alongside display coverage and serious accepted errors.

3. Interactive astronaut-health demonstrator

3.1 Illustrative crew-use scenario

Consider a crew member reviewing an exercise interval during a long-duration mission. A plausible optical candidate is available, but the retrospective reliability decision does not meet the acceptance rule. The interface marks the interval Review Required and withholds the candidate rather than presenting it as an established heart rate. The crew member can record perceived energy, recent sleep duration, exercise context and reported symptoms, creating a structured summary for later review.

A future validated version could support repeat measurement or verification with an approved reference device under established mission medical procedures. The current application illustrates this workflow using terrestrial research outputs and simulated check-ins, not live astronaut telemetry.

3.2 Recorded-data exploration

The public monitoring console lets users select exercise recordings, navigate 20-second windows and compare precomputed raw and motion-separated candidates. It displays descriptive signal-quality information and three retrospective statuses: Cautious Display (the research rule accepts a candidate), Review Required (the rule rejects it) and No Reading (no usable candidate is available). The accepted label does not imply clinical verification.

3.3 Local sensor experiment

A separate JavaScript analyzer accepts a compatible 20-second CSV of synchronized PPG and three-axis acceleration, processing the file locally in the browser without uploading it to a server. It reports exploratory raw and separated frequency candidates, motion-predictability information and temporal-consistency descriptors. This browser approximation does not execute the trained ExtraTrees classifier or provide validated heart-rate decisions on newly uploaded data.

The research replay shows the participant-held-out decisions evaluated offline; the local analyzer demonstrates signal processing on an additional input without applying the evaluated error-risk classifier.

4. Study data and evaluation design

The investigation uses the Wrist PPG During Exercise database from PhysioNet (Casson, 2017; Jarchi and Casson, 2017). The analyzed development subset contains eight participants, 19 terrestrial recordings and 332 non-overlapping, 20-second windows across walking, running, low-resistance cycling and high-resistance cycling. Three windows lack usable paired candidates, leaving 329 windows for the direct raw-versus-separated comparison.

ECG reference measurements define retrospective errors and supervised training labels; they are not inputs to sensor-only extraction. In the outer leave-one-participant-out evaluation, an entire participant is excluded from model fitting. An additional participant-held-out procedure within the remaining participants establishes the acceptance threshold without using labels from the excluded participant.

This design limits direct participant leakage. The same overall dataset informed prior development, however, so the results remain retrospective participant-held-out development findings rather than untouched external validation.

5. Experimental findings

5.1 Paired candidate comparison

Raw strongest spectral peak — 329 windows with candidates; mean absolute error: 36.35 bpm.

Motion-separated spectral peak — 329 windows with candidates; mean absolute error: 21.69 bpm.

Table 1. Both candidate methods were compared on the same 329 eligible analysis windows.

Across these paired windows, motion-aware separation reduced average error by 14.66 bpm. In the archived analysis, 179 candidate windows improved, 96 worsened and 54 were tied. Motion processing therefore helped more often than it hurt in this development set, without making every interval more accurate.

5.2 Reliability-based reporting

Total analysis windows: 332.

Candidate-eligible windows: 329.

Displayed windows / all-window coverage: 125 / 37.7%.

Conditional mean absolute error: 3.62 bpm.

Serious errors (absolute ECG discrepancy at least 15 bpm): 8 of 125 displayed (6.4%).

Table 2. The guarded policy reports conditional accuracy only for accepted readings, not continuous accuracy over all 332 windows.

The raw and separated baselines each cover 329 eligible candidates; the guarded conditional MAE describes 125 accepted windows. The three errors therefore do not refer to identical displayed subsets. An earlier development policy displayed 54 of 332 windows (16.3% coverage), with 21.07 bpm conditional MAE and 16 serious errors; the later participant-held-out policy displayed 125 windows (37.7%), with 3.62 bpm conditional MAE and eight serious errors. Because the policies accepted different windows, this is a descriptive comparison rather than a paired estimate of improvement.

5.3 Statistical uncertainty

Multiple windows were recorded from each participant. To describe between-participant variability, the archived analysis reports 95% participant-cluster bootstrap intervals from 300 resamples:

All-window display coverage: 37.7%; descriptive 95% interval: 20.66–49.53%.

Conditional MAE: 3.62 bpm; descriptive 95% interval: 1.94–5.07 bpm.

Serious-error fraction among displays: 6.4%; descriptive 95% interval: 2.69–8.79%.

Table 3. Intervals describe variability within the eight-person development sample; they do not establish performance in a new population.

5.4 Performance by activity

High-resistance cycling — 51/63 displayed (81.0%); conditional MAE 1.49 bpm; 0 serious errors.

Low-resistance cycling — 44/87 displayed (50.6%); conditional MAE 3.68 bpm; 1 serious error.

Walking — 28/109 displayed (25.7%); conditional MAE 6.46 bpm; 6 serious errors.

Running — 2/73 displayed (2.7%); conditional MAE 16.82 bpm; 1 serious error.

Table 4. Coverage includes all ECG-referenced windows for each activity; error is calculated among displayed readings.

High-resistance cycling produced 51 accepted readings without a serious error. Walking accounted for six of the eight serious accepted errors. Running remained particularly problematic: two of 73 windows were displayed and one contained a serious error. The aggregate conditional MAE obscures these large activity-related differences.

5.5 Scientific interpretation

Acceleration-informed separation improved the average candidate estimate, but its remaining error was substantial. Risk-based selection concentrated the lower-error candidates among the displayed subset, at the cost of sharply reduced availability during running.

The results show why evaluation of a monitoring decision requires conditional accuracy, display coverage, residual serious errors and activity-dependent failures. Each measure captures a different consequence for the person interpreting the reading.

6. Originality and engineering contribution

Motion-artifact removal and PPG signal-quality analysis are established research areas (Ismail, Akram and Siddiqi, 2021; Jarchi and Casson, 2017). Pulsar builds on those approaches by examining the downstream reporting decision on the same exercise development corpus.

The engineering contribution is the linked evaluation of candidate extraction and selective reporting. Raw and acceleration-informed estimates are compared on paired windows; the reliability policy is evaluated with held-out participants and training-derived thresholds. Display coverage, serious accepted errors and activity-specific results reveal the practical consequences of withholding uncertain readings.

The interactive application communicates accepted, withheld and unavailable states through a crew-oriented check-in. The contribution is specific to this implementation and evaluation; the study does not establish superiority over all existing PPG quality-assessment methods.

7. NASA resources and spaceflight relevance

NASA Human Research Program resources on the Five Hazards of Human Spaceflight, Human Spaceflight Risks and ongoing research provide the mission rationale. Altered gravity and cardiovascular adaptation make physiological exercise monitoring relevant; increasing distance from Earth motivates explicit uncertainty and a structured self-assessment pathway when immediate ground support may not be available (NASA Human Research Program, n.d.-a, n.d.-b, n.d.-c).

Pulsar also uses descriptive historical exercise information from NASA’s Exercise Overview technical brief (OCHMO-TB-031, 2023), including average exercise heart rates of approximately 135 bpm for the ISS CEVIS cycle ergometer and 131 bpm for the T2 treadmill. These appear as contextual references in the application, not safety thresholds, training labels or evidence of astronaut validation.

The roles of the sources are distinct: NASA research informs the challenge relevance and the crew-facing experience; PhysioNet supplies the terrestrial PPG, acceleration and ECG recordings used in the quantified experiments.

8. Software implementation and transparency

The scientific work uses Python for signal filtering, spectral analysis, nonlinear accelerometer-derived features, blocked regression, ExtraTrees error-risk modelling and participant-held-out evaluation. The web application is built with HTML, CSS and JavaScript, including SVG-based plots, recorded-result exploration, local CSV processing and simulated crew check-in summaries.

The interactive project is publicly viewable at beautyi122.github.io/pulsar-space-apps-2026/. The research display includes aggregate outcomes, activity-specific results and failure cases. Recorded decisions are distinguished from the exploratory outputs of new browser-local sensor files.

The separately prepared scientific package records 34 manifest-listed files passing SHA-256 integrity checks. Its saved-data reliability experiment reproduced the archived results, and separate recalculation from 332 stored window records confirmed the displayed count, conditional MAE and serious-error total. This verification concerns the saved-data analysis; the original waveform-to-candidate pipeline was not rerun end-to-end in that audit. Public availability of the package is separate from the public website.

9. Limitations, next investigation and potential impact

The development study included eight terrestrial participants with repeated measurement windows, so its findings cannot be generalized directly to astronauts or clinical monitoring. The classifier scores are uncalibrated, eight displayed readings had serious errors, and running coverage was inadequate. The browser demonstrator does not deploy the offline trained risk model. Neither astronaut testing nor independent external clinical validation has occurred.

The next scientific test is to freeze the algorithm and acceptance policy before evaluation on new participants, sensor devices and movement conditions, especially when arm cadence overlaps pulse frequency. That study should jointly assess coverage and serious errors and examine whether users correctly interpret uncertainty notices.

The same measurement-integrity problem occurs in terrestrial rehabilitation and supervised exercise. Repetitive arm movements may distort optical pulse estimates; a future validated system could flag questionable intervals for confirmation before they are used to interpret physiological changes. Clinical benefit has not been evaluated in this project.

For astronauts, the corresponding potential is a clearer distinction between a usable measurement, an uncertain measurement requiring review and an interval where the sensor provides insufficient evidence. That could contribute to more informed self-assessment during distant missions, subject to rigorous mission-specific validation.

10. Conclusion

Pulsar evaluated motion-aware pulse estimation and a separate selective-reporting policy on terrestrial exercise recordings. Paired candidate comparisons showed lower average spectral error after separation. Participant-held-out reliability selection produced lower conditional error among accepted readings but retained serious mistakes and very low running coverage.

During distant missions, a persuasive-looking sensor value can be less useful than a clear indication that further verification is needed. Pulsar offers a tested research framework for examining that decision and a crew-facing demonstration of how its uncertainty could be communicated.
